title: Ministers of a New Covenant: Letter, Spirit, and the Veil
summary: Paul needs no letters of recommendation: the Corinthian believers themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts. God has made him competent as a minister of a new covenant, whose glory surpasses the glory that shone from Moses' face when the law was given. The veil that Moses wore, and that still lies over hearts when the old covenant is read, is removed when anyone turns to the Lord, and believers, beholding the Lord's glory, are being transformed into his image.
story: Chapter 2 ended with a question: "who is qualified for such a task?" This chapter answers it. Paul's competence comes from God, who has made him a minister of the new covenant promised by the prophets. To explain what is new about it, Paul goes back to the story of Moses coming down from Mount Sinai with the tablets of the law, his face shining (Exodus 34:29-35). The chapter continues the defense of Paul's ministry that runs from 2:14 to 7:4, and it lays the foundation for chapter 4, where the same themes of glory, veil, and seeing continue.
historical:
Paul's opponents in Corinth, whose full profile appears in chapters 10-13, seem to have arrived with letters of recommendation and to have questioned whether Paul had any. They may also have made much of their Jewish credentials (11:22), which may be why Paul turns to Moses and the covenant at Sinai. The chapter should not be read as an attack on the Jewish people; Paul speaks as a Jew about his own people's Scriptures, and his hope is that the veil will be taken away.

The new covenant was promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34, where God says he will put his law within his people and write it on their hearts, and in Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26-27, where God promises to remove the heart of stone, give a heart of flesh, and put his Spirit within them. Jesus spoke of the cup at the Last Supper as the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). Paul's phrases "tablets of stone" and "tablets of human hearts" in verse 3 draw directly on this prophetic hope.
cultural:
Letters of recommendation were a normal part of ancient life. A traveler arriving in a strange city, a teacher seeking a hearing, or a believer moving between churches would carry a letter from someone trusted, vouching for him. The New Testament contains examples (Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1-2), and much of Paul's letter to Philemon works this way. In a city like Corinth, where status and patronage mattered, such letters signaled who a person was connected to. Paul's reply is that a living community created by the gospel is better proof than any document.

The account in Exodus 34 tells that when Moses came down from the mountain, the skin of his face shone because he had been speaking with the LORD, and the Israelites were afraid to come near. Moses put a veil over his face when he spoke with the people and removed it when he went in before the LORD. Paul reads this closely. He says the glory was fading or being brought to an end (the verb can mean either, and Exodus does not itself say the glory faded), and he uses the veil as a picture of a hardness that keeps readers from seeing where the old covenant was leading. The weekly reading of the law in the synagogue is in view in verses 14-15.
literary: The chapter is built on contrasts: ink and Spirit, stone and hearts, letter and Spirit, death and life, condemnation and righteousness, fading and enduring. Verses 7-11 use a classic Jewish form of argument from the lesser to the greater ("how much more"), three times over. The old covenant had real glory, Paul insists; the new covenant has more. Verses 12-18 then work like a short commentary on Exodus 34, moving from Moses' veil to the veil over readers' hearts, and then to verse 16, which echoes the wording of Exodus 34:34 (Moses turning to the LORD and removing the veil) and applies it to anyone who turns to the Lord. The chapter ends with a single sentence (verse 18) that gathers every image: unveiled faces, reflected glory, image, transformation, and the Spirit.

outline.t: The Corinthians are Paul's letter, written by the Spirit
Competence from God for a new covenant
The surpassing glory of the ministry of the Spirit
Moses' veil and the veil removed in Christ
Freedom, unveiled faces, and transformation by the Spirit

doctrines.note: The chapter contrasts the covenant given at Sinai, written on stone, with the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and Ezekiel, written by the Spirit on hearts. The old covenant had glory; the new surpasses it because it gives life and righteousness, not only commands.

The Spirit writes on hearts, gives life, brings freedom, and transforms believers into the Lord's image. Verse 17, "the Lord is the Spirit", is read by some as Paul explaining that the "Lord" of Exodus 34 whom Moses faced is, in the new covenant, encountered as the Spirit, and by others as a close identification of the risen Lord's presence with the Spirit's work. Neither reading erases the distinction between them, since verse 18 speaks of the Lord who is the Spirit and verse 17 of the Spirit of the Lord.

Paul calls the law's ministry a ministry "of death" and "of condemnation" not because the law is evil but because, written on stone, it could command without giving the power to obey. "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (verse 6) contrasts the law as external code with the Spirit's inner renewal; it is not a rule about reading Scripture literally or figuratively.

words.note: Diatheke, covenant. In ordinary Greek it could mean a will or testament, but in the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew berit, the binding relationship God establishes with his people. This is the source of the names Old and New Testament. Verse 6 is one of the few places in Paul's letters where he explicitly calls his work the ministry of the new covenant.

Gramma, something written, a letter of the alphabet or a written text. In verse 6 it stands for the law as inscribed code, written on stone. Paul's contrast is between what is merely written outside a person and what the Spirit writes within, not between literal and allegorical interpretation.

Kalymma, veil or covering. It appears four times in verses 13-16, first of Moses' literal veil and then of the covering over hearts and minds. The veil does not belong to the old covenant Scriptures themselves but to the way they are read without Christ.

Metamorphoo, to be transformed, changed in form (the root of the English word metamorphosis). The same verb describes Jesus' transfiguration (Matthew 17:2) and the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2). Here it is in the present tense and passive: believers are being transformed, gradually, by the Spirit, into Christ's image.

christ: The chapter shows Christ as the one in whom the old covenant finds its goal and its meaning. The veil over the reading of Moses is removed "only in Christ" (verse 14), so that the whole of Scripture comes into focus when read in his light. The new covenant that Jeremiah promised is the covenant Jesus sealed in his blood. The glory that shone on Moses' face was real but temporary; the glory believers now see is the Lord's own, and they are "being transformed into His image" (verse 18). Chapter 4 will say plainly whose image this is: Christ, "who is the image of God" (4:4), in whose face God's glory shines (4:6).

hard.q: Does Paul dismiss the Old Testament and the Jewish people when he speaks of a ministry of death and a veil over their hearts?
hard.a:
The language is strong, and it has been misused to support contempt for Jews. But the chapter itself resists that use. Paul insists that the old covenant came with glory, so much that the Israelites could not look at Moses' face. He argues that the new covenant is greater, not that the old was worthless. He calls the law's ministry one of death and condemnation because the law, however good, could not by itself change hearts, a point Romans 7:12-14 makes while calling the law holy and spiritual.

The veil, in Paul's reading, is not a permanent verdict on a people but a condition that can be removed, and he expects it to be: "whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away". Paul writes as a Jew who once read Moses the same way, and Romans 9-11 shows his anguished hope for his own people. Readers today differ on how to describe the relationship between Israel and the church, and between the old and new covenants, but a reading of this chapter that breeds contempt for the Jewish people contradicts the apostle who wrote it.

questions: Paul says the Corinthians are a letter from Christ known and read by everyone. What would a watching neighbor read in the life of your church?
What is the difference between knowing God's commands on the outside and having them written on the heart? Where have you experienced each?
Transformation in verse 18 happens gradually, as believers behold the Lord's glory. What does that suggest about how people really change?
